characters.name: Mathieu
characters.personality: chatty, always first at the coffee machine, curious about how you are settling in

characters.name: Hélène
characters.personality: friendly and direct, talks fast and loves office jargon

characters.name: Léa
characters.personality: sporty, enthusiastic; a classmate from your Wednesday drawing class

characters.name: Gérard
characters.personality: café owner, born in Lyon, proud of the places tourists never find

characters.name: Hugo
characters.personality: good-humoured, loves a friendly argument, grew up in a Beaujolais village

characters.name: Camille
characters.personality: warm, cheerful, always in a rush; your friend from chapters 1 and 2, eager to hear your news

notes: Tu between colleagues of the same level (Mathieu) and with friends (Léa, Hugo, and Camille, who returns from chapters 1 and 2); vous with the team lead Hélène at the first meeting and with Gérard, the café owner. Please confirm tu with a colleague in the first week feels natural.

The learner keeps the chapter-1 name Sam and the masculine default (fatigué, crevé, ravi, perdu, sorti); feminine forms are given in the notes. Sam's job, graphiste, is the same word for a man or a woman.
Wordings to check first: « dans la boîte », « Vous faites plutôt du print ou du web ? », « faire un point », « je suis fan de vélo », « Il était minuit. Enfin, onze heures, je veux dire. ».
Facts to verify: the Croix-Rousse market open every morning except Monday, metro C two stops from Hôtel de Ville to Croix-Rousse, the traboules of Vieux-Lyon.

titles.en: A coffee break with a colleague

scene.en: The coffee machine at the design agency near Part-Dieu where you have just started; your colleague Mathieu wants to know how your days go.

lines.text: Salut ! Alors, cette première semaine, ça se passe bien ?
lines.pron: Semaine: suh-MEN. Ça se passe: sah suh PASS.

en.m: Hi! So, is your first week going well?
en.n: Colleagues of the same level usually say tu to each other in French offices. Ça se passe bien ? (is it going well?) works for a job, a trip or a meal.
en.l: hi! so, this first week, that itself passes well

lines.text: Ça va, mais je suis un peu fatigué.
lines.pron: Fatigué: fah-tee-GAY. Un peu: uhn PUH.

en.m: It's OK, but I'm a bit tired.
en.n: A woman writes fatiguée; it sounds the same. Un peu (a little) softens a complaint: un peu stressé, un peu perdu.
en.l: that goes, but I am a little tired

lines.text: Ah bon ? Tu te lèves à quelle heure ?
lines.pron: Lèves: lev. Quelle heure runs together: keh-LUHR.

en.m: Really? What time do you get up?
en.n: Se lever (to get up) is reflexive: je me lève, tu te lèves. Ah bon ? is the all-purpose 'really?' that keeps a chat going.
en.l: ah good? you yourself raise at what hour

lines.text: Je me lève à six heures et quart.
lines.pron: Six heures links: see-ZUHR. Quart: kar, with a silent t.

en.m: I get up at a quarter past six.
en.n: Et quart = quarter past, et demie = half past, moins le quart = quarter to. In everyday talk people use the 12-hour clock: six heures du matin.
en.l: I myself raise at six hours and quarter

lines.text: Je prends mon petit-déjeuner, puis le métro.

en.m: I have breakfast, then I take the metro.
en.n: In France le déjeuner is lunch and le petit-déjeuner is breakfast (in Belgium, Switzerland and Quebec, déjeuner is breakfast). Prendre works for meals and transport alike.
en.l: I take my little-lunch, then the metro

lines.text: Et tu fais quoi, exactement, dans la boîte ?

en.m: And what exactly do you do at the company?
en.n: Une boîte (a box) is everyday slang for a company: elle travaille dans une grosse boîte. Tu fais quoi ? is the casual 'what do you do?'.
en.l: and you do what, exactly, in the box

lines.text: Je suis graphiste, dans l’équipe d’Hélène.
lines.pron: Graphiste: grah-FEEST. D’Hélène: day-LEN, the h is silent.

en.m: I'm a graphic designer, on Hélène's team.
en.n: No article before a job after je suis: je suis graphiste, never un graphiste. De becomes d’ before a vowel or a silent h: l’équipe d’Hélène.
en.l: I am graphic-designer, in the team of Hélène

lines.text: Et ce week-end, tu fais quelque chose ?
lines.pron: Week-end is said the French way, stressed at the end: wee-KEND.

en.m: And are you doing anything this weekend?
en.n: French borrowed week-end from English; Quebec says la fin de semaine. Ce week-end = this coming weekend.
en.l: and this weekend, you do something

lines.text: Samedi, je vais faire la grasse matinée !

en.m: On Saturday, I'm going to sleep in!
en.n: Faire la grasse matinée (to do the fat morning) = to sleep in. Aller + infinitive is the near future: je vais faire, on va voir.
en.l: Saturday, I go to-do the fat morning

lines.text: Je suis crevé, mais ça va !

en.m: I'm exhausted, but I'm OK!
en.n: Crevé (literally 'punctured', like a tyre) is the casual word for exhausted; a woman writes crevée. Keep it for friends and colleagues.
en.l: I am punctured, but that goes

scene.en: Your first meeting with Hélène, who leads your team at the agency and was away last week; she is friendly but talks fast and loves jargon.

lines.text: Bonjour ! Hélène Garnier, je dirige l’équipe.

en.m: Hello! Hélène Garnier, I lead the team.
en.n: At work people often introduce themselves with first name and surname, then their role. Diriger une équipe = to lead a team.
en.l: good-day! Hélène Garnier, I direct the team

lines.text: Bonjour, je me présente : Sam Taylor.
lines.pron: Présente: pray-ZAHNT; an s between two vowels sounds like z.

en.m: Hello, let me introduce myself: Sam Taylor.
en.n: Je me présente (I present myself) is the formal way to give your name at work or in a meeting. In writing, French puts a space before a colon.
en.l: good-day, I myself present: Sam Taylor

lines.text: Ravi de faire votre connaissance.

en.m: Pleased to meet you.
en.n: The formal 'pleased to meet you'. A woman writes ravie; it sounds the same. Lighter and very common: enchanté.
en.l: delighted to make your acquaintance

lines.text: Vous faites plutôt du print ou du web ?
lines.pron: Print is said almost as in English, with a French r: preent.

en.m: Do you mostly do print or web?
en.n: Office French borrows many English words: le print (printed work), le web, un mail, une deadline. Plutôt = rather, mostly.
en.l: you do rather some print or some web

lines.text: Je fais surtout du web, mais aussi des affiches.

en.m: I mostly do web work, but posters too.
en.n: Faire du + field = to work in it: faire du web, faire du marketing. Surtout means 'mostly, above all', never 'surely'.
en.l: I do above-all some web, but also some posters

lines.text: Très bien. On fait un point à quinze heures ?
lines.pron: Point: pwan, a nasal vowel with no n or t sound. Quinze: kanz.

en.m: Very good. Shall we have a catch-up at 3 p.m.?
en.n: Faire un point is office French for a short catch-up meeting. Work times use the 24-hour clock: quinze heures = 3 p.m.
en.l: very well. one makes a point at fifteen hours

lines.text: Pardon, que veut dire « faire un point » ?

en.m: Sorry, what does « faire un point » mean?
en.n: Que veut dire… ? or qu’est-ce que ça veut dire ? = what does … mean? Vouloir dire (to want to say) is how French says 'to mean'.
en.l: sorry, what wants to-say « to-make a point »

lines.text: C’est une courte réunion, pour voir où on en est.
lines.pron: Réunion: ray-ü-NYON. Où on en est: oo on-nahn-NAY.

en.m: It's a short meeting to see where we're at.
en.n: False friend: une réunion is a meeting, not a reunion. Où on en est (where one of-it is) = how things stand.
en.l: it is a short meeting, for to-see where one of-it is

lines.text: D’accord. Je dois préparer quelque chose ?
lines.pron: Préparer: pray-pah-RAY. Quelque chose: kel-kuh SHOHZ.

en.m: OK. Do I need to prepare anything?
en.n: Devoir + infinitive = to have to: je dois préparer. A statement said with a rising voice is the simplest polite question.
en.l: of agreement. I must to-prepare some thing

lines.text: En attendant, je peux m’installer ici ?

en.m: In the meantime, can I set up here?
en.n: S’installer = to settle in, to take a seat or a desk. Je peux… ? is the everyday way to ask permission; more formal: est-ce que je pourrais… ?
en.l: in waiting, I can myself install here

lines.text: Bonjour, je suis Sam, le nouveau graphiste.

en.m: Hello, I'm Sam, the new graphic designer.
en.n: Less formal and just as common. A woman says la nouvelle graphiste: the article and the adjective change, the job title does not.
en.l: good-day, I am Sam, the new graphic-designer

titles.en: What do you do for fun?

scene.en: After your Wednesday evening drawing class at the local community centre, your classmate Léa asks what you do at weekends; it turns out you share a passion.

lines.text: Et le week-end, tu fais quoi, en général ?

en.m: And what do you usually do at weekends?
en.n: In casual French the question word often comes last: tu fais quoi ? En général = usually.
en.l: and the weekend, you do what, in general

lines.text: Le samedi, je fais souvent du vélo.

en.m: On Saturdays, I often go cycling.
en.n: Le samedi (with le) = on Saturdays, every week; samedi alone = this Saturday. Faire du + sport: faire du vélo, du tennis, de la natation.
en.l: the Saturday, I do often some bike

lines.text: C’est vrai ? Moi aussi, je suis fan de vélo !
lines.pron: Fan is said as in English. Vrai: vreh.

en.m: Really? Me too, I'm a big cycling fan!
en.n: Être fan de = to be a big fan of, very common among younger French speakers. Moi aussi = me too; moi non plus = me neither.
en.l: it is true? me also, I am fan of bike

lines.text: J’adore rouler sur les quais du Rhône.
lines.pron: Rouler: roo-LAY. Quais: kay. Rhône: rohn.

en.m: I love riding along the banks of the Rhône.
en.n: Adorer + infinitive = to love doing. Cyclists and drivers say rouler (to roll) for riding. Lyon's riverbanks, les quais, have long car-free paths.
en.l: I adore to-roll on the quays of-the Rhône

lines.text: Par contre, je déteste monter à la Croix-Rousse !

en.m: On the other hand, I hate riding up to the Croix-Rousse!
en.n: Par contre = on the other hand. The Croix-Rousse is the steep hill just north of the city centre, dreaded by Lyon's cyclists. Détester + infinitive = to hate doing.
en.l: by against, I detest to-climb to the Cross-Red

lines.text: Ha ha, moi aussi ! Et le soir, plutôt films ou livres ?

en.m: Ha ha, me too! And in the evening, films or books?
en.n: Plutôt X ou Y ? (rather X or Y?) is the quick way to ask about someone's tastes, with no verb at all.
en.l: ha ha, me also! and the evening, rather films or books

lines.text: Je préfère les films, surtout en VO.

en.m: I prefer films, especially in the original language.
en.n: En VO (version originale) = in the original language with subtitles; en VF = dubbed into French. Préférer takes the article: je préfère les films.
en.l: I prefer the films, above-all in OV

lines.text: Et toi, tu préfères quoi ?

en.m: What about you, which do you prefer?
en.n: Et toi ? hands the question back; to someone you say vous to: et vous ?
en.l: and you, you prefer what

lines.text: Moi, les livres ! Je lis tous les soirs dans le tram.
lines.pron: Lis: lee. Tous les soirs: too lay SWAHR.

en.m: Books, for me! I read every evening on the tram.
en.n: Starting with moi puts the stress on 'me', the way English does with the voice. Tous les soirs = every evening.
en.l: me, the books! I read all the evenings in the tram

lines.text: On fait une balade à vélo dimanche ?

en.m: Shall we go for a bike ride on Sunday?
en.n: Une balade = a ride or a walk for pleasure: une balade à pied, à vélo, en bateau. On fait… ? is how friends suggest a plan.
en.l: one does a ride at bike Sunday

lines.text: J’aime mieux les films que les livres.

en.m: I like films better than books.
en.n: Aimer mieux X que Y = to like X better than Y, a little more relaxed than préférer.
en.l: I love better the films than the books

scene.en: A small café near Place des Terreaux; Gérard, the owner, was born in Lyon and knows the places tourists never find.

lines.text: Pardon, monsieur, je peux vous demander un conseil ?
lines.pron: Monsieur: muh-SYUH. Conseil: kon-SAY, ending in a light y.

en.m: Excuse me, sir, can I ask you for some advice?
en.n: Pardon works like 'excuse me' to get someone's attention. Un conseil = a piece of advice; the plural des conseils is common.
en.l: pardon, sir, I can you ask an advice

lines.text: Qu’est-ce qu’il faut voir à Lyon, d’après vous ?
lines.pron: Il faut: eel FOH. D’après: dah-PREH.

en.m: What should I see in Lyon, in your opinion?
en.n: Il faut + infinitive = one must, you have to: il faut voir, il faut goûter. D’après vous = in your opinion.
en.l: what is-it that it is-needed to-see at Lyon, from-after you

lines.text: Allez au marché de la Croix-Rousse, un dimanche matin.

en.m: Go to the Croix-Rousse market on a Sunday morning.
en.n: The Croix-Rousse market stretches along the boulevard every morning except Monday; Sunday is its liveliest day.
en.l: go to-the market of the Cross-Red, a Sunday morning

lines.text: Ah bon ? Pourquoi celui-là ?

en.m: Really? Why that one?
en.n: Celui-là = that one, for a masculine noun (le marché); celle-là for a feminine one.
en.l: ah good? why that-one-there

lines.text: C’est le marché des Lyonnais, pas des touristes !

en.m: It's where the people of Lyon shop, not the tourists!
en.n: Les Lyonnais = the people of Lyon. In quick speech pas alone can negate a single word: pas des touristes.
en.l: it is the market of-the Lyonnais, not of-the tourists

lines.text: Il est ouvert tous les jours ?
lines.pron: Ouvert: oo-VAIR, silent t. Tous les jours: too lay ZHOOR.

en.m: Is it open every day?
en.n: Ouvert / fermé = open / closed. Many French shops and markets close on Sunday afternoon or on Monday, so it is always worth asking.
en.l: it is open all the days

lines.text: Tous les matins, sauf le lundi.

en.m: Every morning, except Mondays.
en.n: Sauf = except. Le lundi with le = on Mondays, every week.
en.l: all the mornings, except the Monday

lines.text: Et comment est-ce qu’on y va, d’ici ?
lines.pron: Comment est-ce qu’on y va: ko-mahn ess-kon-nee VAH.

en.m: And how do you get there from here?
en.n: Y = there: on y va = one goes there. Est-ce que turns a statement into a question without changing the word order.
en.l: and how is-it that one there goes, from-here

lines.text: C’est loin, à pied ?

en.m: Is it far on foot?
en.n: À pied = on foot; en métro = by metro, en bus = by bus.
en.l: it is far, at foot

lines.text: Non, mais ça monte ! Prenez le métro C, c’est deux arrêts.

en.m: No, but it's uphill! Take metro line C, it's two stops.
en.n: Ça monte = it's uphill. Metro line C climbs from Hôtel de Ville up to Croix-Rousse; it is a rack railway, built for the steep slope.
en.l: no, but that climbs! take the metro C, it is two stops

lines.text: Merci beaucoup pour vos conseils !

en.m: Thanks a lot for your advice!
en.n: Merci pour + noun: merci pour vos conseils, merci pour tout. Advice is countable in French, so it is plural here.
en.l: thanks much for your advices

lines.text: Vous me conseillez quoi, pour ce week-end ?

en.m: What would you recommend for this weekend?
en.n: Conseiller quelque chose à quelqu’un = to recommend something to someone. Quoi at the end sounds relaxed but stays polite with vous.
en.l: you to-me advise what, for this weekend

scene.en: Over a drink on a terrace by the Saône, your friend Hugo, who grew up in a Beaujolais village, insists the countryside beats the city.

lines.text: Franchement, la campagne, c’est mieux que la ville !

en.m: Honestly, the countryside is better than the city!
en.n: Franchement (frankly) opens many opinions among friends. Mieux (better) is the everyday comparative of bien: c’est mieux que…
en.l: frankly, the countryside, it is better than the town

lines.text: Je ne suis pas tout à fait d’accord.
lines.pron: Tout à fait: too-tah-FEH; the t of tout links to à.

en.m: I don't quite agree.
en.n: Pas tout à fait = not quite: a soft way to disagree. Plain je ne suis pas d’accord is fine too, just blunter.
en.l: I not am not all at made of agreement

lines.text: Moi, je trouve la ville plus pratique.

en.m: Personally, I find the city more convenient.
en.n: Je trouve (I find) is the most common way to give an opinion: je trouve ça cher. False friend: pratique means convenient, handy, not only 'practical'.
en.l: me, I find the town more practical

lines.text: Ah bon ? Et pourquoi ?

en.m: Oh really? Why's that?
en.n: Ah bon ? shows surprise, like 'oh, really?', and invites a reason.
en.l: ah good? and why

lines.text: Parce qu’on peut tout faire à pied ou en métro.

en.m: Because you can do everything on foot or by metro.
en.n: Parce que (because) becomes parce qu’ before a vowel. On is the general 'you' here. Tout goes before the infinitive: tout faire.
en.l: because that one can all to-do at foot or in metro

lines.text: Oui, mais en ville, les loyers sont beaucoup trop chers !

en.m: Yes, but in the city, rents are far too high!
en.n: Le loyer = the rent. Trop = too; beaucoup trop = far too. Rents in Lyon are among the highest in France outside Paris.
en.l: yes, but in town, the rents are much too expensive

lines.text: Là, je suis d’accord avec toi.
lines.pron: D’accord: dah-KOR. Avec toi: ah-vek TWAH.

en.m: On that, I agree with you.
en.n: Là (there) = on that point. Être d’accord avec quelqu’un = to agree with someone; d’accord on its own means OK.
en.l: there, I am of agreement with you

lines.text: Mais pour le travail, tu en penses quoi ?

en.m: But what about work, what do you think?
en.n: Penser de = to think of (an opinion). En stands for 'of it': tu en penses quoi ? = what do you think of it?
en.l: but for the work, you of-it think what

lines.text: C’est vrai, c’est plus facile en ville. Un point pour toi !

en.m: True, it's easier in the city. A point to you!
en.n: Un point pour toi ! = one point to you: a playful way to give in during a friendly argument.
en.l: it is true, it is more easy in town. a point for you

lines.text: À mon avis, la ville, c’est mieux.

en.m: In my opinion, the city is better.
en.n: À mon avis = in my opinion. False friend: un avis is an opinion; a piece of advice is un conseil.
en.l: at my opinion, the town, it is better

scene.en: Camille, your friend since your first days in Lyon, meets you for a coffee; you tell her how you got lost in the old town last night.

lines.text: Tu sais quoi ? Hier soir, je me suis perdu !
lines.pron: Hier: yair, one syllable. Perdu: pair-DÜ.

en.m: Guess what? I got lost last night!
en.n: Se perdre (to get lost) takes être in the passé composé: je me suis perdu. A woman writes perdue; it sounds the same. Tu sais quoi ? = guess what?
en.l: you know what? yesterday evening, I myself am lost

lines.text: Perdu ? Comment ça ?

en.m: Lost? What do you mean?
en.n: Comment ça ? = what do you mean? how so? Repeating a word with a rising voice asks for more.
en.l: lost? how that

lines.text: J’ai pris une traboule dans le Vieux-Lyon, et je suis sorti ailleurs.

en.m: I took a traboule in the old town and came out somewhere else.
en.n: Traboules are passages through buildings and courtyards, a Lyon speciality. Prendre → j’ai pris (with avoir); sortir → je suis sorti (with être; a woman writes sortie).
en.l: I have taken a traboule in the Old-Lyon, and I am gone-out elsewhere

lines.text: Oh non ! Il était quelle heure ?

en.m: Oh no! What time was it?
en.n: Il était (it was) is the imperfect: it sets the scene in a story, while the passé composé tells what happened.
en.l: oh no! it was what hour

lines.text: Il était minuit. Enfin, onze heures, je veux dire.

en.m: It was midnight. Well, eleven, I mean.
en.n: Enfin (literally 'finally') also corrects what you have just said, like 'well'. Je veux dire = I mean.
en.l: it was midnight. finally, eleven hours, I want to-say

lines.text: Heureusement, un monsieur m’a aidé.

en.m: Luckily, a man helped me.
en.n: Heureusement = luckily. M’a aidé = helped me: the object pronoun comes before avoir. Un monsieur is a polite way to say 'a man'.
en.l: happily, a sir me has helped

lines.text: Ah, sympa ! Et qu’est-ce qu’il t’a dit ?
lines.pron: Sympa: san-PAH. Il t’a dit: eel tah DEE.

en.m: Oh, nice! And what did he say?
en.n: Sympa (short for sympathique) = nice, friendly. False friend: sympathique never means 'sympathetic'.
en.l: ah, nice! and what is-it that he to-you has said

lines.text: Il connaissait un « shortcut ». Comment on dit ça en français ?
lines.pron: Connaissait: koh-neh-SEH. On dit: on DEE.

en.m: He knew a shortcut. How do you say that in French?
en.n: Comment on dit… en français ? is the question to keep asking. Connaître (to know a person or a place) → il connaissait, the imperfect.
en.l: he knew a « shortcut ». how one says that in French

lines.text: Un raccourci ! Tu as eu de la chance.

en.m: A shortcut! You were lucky.
en.n: Un raccourci comes from court (short). False friend: avoir de la chance = to be lucky; 'a chance' is une occasion.
en.l: a shortcut! you have had of the luck

lines.text: La prochaine fois, je prendrai le métro !

en.m: Next time, I'll take the metro!
en.n: Prendrai is the future of prendre: drop the final e of the infinitive and add -ai. La prochaine fois = next time.
en.l: the next time, I will-take the metro

lines.text: Comment ça s’appelle, en français ?

en.m: What's it called in French?
en.n: Ça s’appelle (it calls itself) = it's called: the same verb as je m’appelle. Point at the thing as you ask.
en.l: how that itself calls, in French
